title: The Question You Skip Is the One That Decides It
author: Say It Well
summary: This piece by Say It Well distills Harvard Business School researcher Alison Wood Brooks' question-asking studies into a practical playbook for high-stakes conversations like job interviews. Drawing on a hand-labeled analysis of 368 transcripts, Brooks' team found that follow-up questions, not a prepared list of topics, account for nearly all of the measurable social benefit of asking questions, and a re-analysis of a Stanford speed-dating dataset showed that a single extra question per encounter reliably produced one additional positive outcome. The article walks through Brooks' taxonomy of question types, showing that introductory and mirror questions do little for likability while follow-ups function as what she calls the 'superheroes of conversation.' It also surfaces a less commonly discussed reason people skip questions: apathy, particularly among those who hold more status than the person they are speaking with. The piece closes with a concrete method: set a floor of five questions before any important conversation, follow up on the interlocutor's own words rather than switching topics, and disclose something of your own thinking to avoid seeming like you are interrogating rather than conversing.
points: Brooks' hand-labeled analysis of 368 transcripts found follow-up questions make up 44% of natural conversation, and nearly all of the measurable benefit of question-asking comes from follow-ups rather than a prepared list.

Across a re-analyzed 2013 Stanford speed-dating dataset (110 daters, 2,000+ conversations), asking just one additional question per date produced one additional "yes," turning a nearly free behavior into a measurable outcome.
Mirror questions (reciprocating "how are you") and introductory questions don't move the likability needle despite persisting at a steady rate throughout conversations; only follow-ups do.
Brooks names apathy, alongside ego and fear of appearing intrusive, as a third reason people, especially those with more status, fail to ask questions.
Her practical prescription is small: set a floor of at least five questions, follow up on the specific words the other person used, and disclose something about yourself between questions.
quotes: Nine research assistants read through a sample of 368 transcripts and hand-labeled the question types. They found six: introductory, mirror, full-switch, partial-switch, follow-up, and rhetorical. Follow-ups made up 44% of all questions asked, more than any other type.

Brooks describes follow-up questions as the superheroes of conversation. They are the opposite of topic-switching questions, since they hold you on the present subject and probe deeper into something the other person already said.
Researchers found that a participant who asked just one more question on each of their 20 dates would get one additional yes across those dates, on average. One question. One extra outcome.

Brooks also names two question types that do nothing for you. Introductory questions open a conversation and are necessary. Mirror questions reciprocate what was just asked, as in answering "how are you" and returning it, and her research found the likability boost applies to neither.

Apathy. A potential questioner, such as a manager, may simply not care about the answers, feeling disinterest in what the other person has to say. Her response to that is direct: the apathy is often misplaced, since we have much to learn from others and perhaps especially from people lower in status than ourselves.

Set an explicit number before you walk in. Her advice is to go into the conversation thinking you need to ask at least five questions, or that you need to ask questions, listen to the answers, and ask follow-ups.
